findings.title: Failure threshold opens an incident without enough failures
findings.body: try_incident_threshold only treats the failure_issue_threshold window as "not yet an incident" when one of the fetched check-ins is OK. It never requires that window to actually contain failure_issue_threshold failed check-ins. The query is sliced to that many rows and then, if none are OK, the environment is saved as MonitorStatus.ERROR, a MonitorIncident is created, and issue occurrences are emitted. A monitor configured with failure_issue_threshold=3 and only one failed check-in (typical for a new monitor, or any history shorter than the threshold) therefore fails immediately. Non-failure statuses other than OK, such as in-progress, also do not block this path and still occupy slots in the slice, so the real failure count can be below the threshold even when the slice is full. If the slice is empty, the same path still persists ERROR and then raises IndexError on previous_checkins[0], leaving the environment failed with no incident and later failures stuck on the already-ERROR branch, which does not create one. Before saving status or calling get_or_create, require a full window whose every status is a real failure (error, missed, or timeout).

findings.title: Occurrence context drops the prepared schedule_type
findings.body: get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config and, when schedule_type is present, replaces it with monitor.get_schedule_type_display() so the issue event gets a human-readable schedule. The returned context ignores that copy and sends monitor_environment.monitor.config instead. Every monitor incident occurrence therefore keeps the raw stored schedule_type (typically the integer choice value) rather than the display label just computed, and the event payload shares the model’s live config dict instead of a detached copy. Downstream mutation or display of that context will not match what this function prepared. Return the modified config dict.
